# memmap2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/memmap2/

## Expand description

A cross-platform Rust API for memory mapped buffers.

The core functionality is provided by either [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) or

[, which correspond to mapping a](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)

`File`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&[u8]`[respectively. Both function by dereferencing to a slice, allowing the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&mut [u8]`[/](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)

`Mmap`[to be used in the same way you would the equivalent slice types.](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

For simple cases [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) can be used directly:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use memmap2::Mmap;
let mut file = File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?;
let mut contents = Vec::new();
file.read_to_end(&mut contents)?;
let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)?  };
assert_eq!(&contents[..], &mmap[..]);
```
However for cases which require configuration of the mapping, then
you can use [ MmapOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html) in order to further configure a mapping
before you create it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)
- A handle to an immutable memory mapped buffer.
- [MmapMut](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)
- A handle to a mutable memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html)- Options
- A memory map builder, providing advanced options and flags for specifying memory map behavior.
- [MmapRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRaw.html)
- A handle to a raw memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRawDescriptor.html)- RawDescriptor
- [Remap](https://docs.rs/struct.RemapOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `Mmap::remap``MmapMut::remap`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Advice](https://docs.rs/enum.Advice.html)
- Values supported by `Mmap::advise``MmapMut::advise`
- [Unchecked](https://docs.rs/enum.UncheckedAdvice.html)- Advice
- Values supported by `Mmap::unchecked_advise``MmapMut::unchecked_advise`

# memmap2 0.9.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memmap2/latest

# memmap2

A Rust library for cross-platform memory mapped IO.

This is a **fork** of the [memmap-rs](https://github.com/danburkert/memmap-rs) crate.

## Features

- file-backed memory maps
- anonymous memory maps
- synchronous and asynchronous flushing
- copy-on-write memory maps
- read-only memory maps
-  stack support (`MAP_STACK`on unix)
- executable memory maps
- huge page support (linux only)

A list of supported/tested targets can be found in [Actions](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/memmap2-rs/actions).

## License

`memmap2` is primarily distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE), [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

Copyright (c) 2020 Yevhenii Reizner

Copyright (c) 2015 Dan Burkert

# stable_deref_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stable_deref_trait/^1.0/

## Expand description

This module defines an unsafe marker trait, StableDeref, for container types that deref to a fixed address which is valid even when the containing type is moved. For example, Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String implement this trait. Additionally, it defines CloneStableDeref for types like Rc where clones deref to the same address.

It is intended to be used by crates such as [owning_ref](https://crates.io/crates/owning_ref) and [rental](https://crates.io/crates/rental), as well as library authors who wish to make their code interoperable with such crates. For example, if you write a custom Vec type, you can implement StableDeref, and then users will be able to use your custom type together with owning_ref and rental.

no_std support can be enabled by disabling default features (specifically “std”). In this case, the trait will not be implemented for the std types mentioned above, but you can still use it for your own types.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clone](https://docs.rs/trait.CloneStableDeref.html)- Stable - Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types where clones deref to the same address. This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableDeref.html)- Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types that deref to a stable address, even when moved. For example, this is implemented by Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String, among others. Even when a Box is moved, the underlying storage remains at a fixed location.

# owning_ref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/owning_ref/^0.4.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#an-owning-reference)An owning reference.

This crate provides the *owning reference* types `OwningRef` and `OwningRefMut`
that enables it to bundle a reference together with the owner of the data it points to.
This allows moving and dropping of a `OwningRef` without needing to recreate the reference.

This can sometimes be useful because Rust borrowing rules normally prevent moving a type that has been moved from. For example, this kind of code gets rejected:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn return_owned_and_referenced<'a>() -> (Vec<u8>, &'a [u8]) {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let s = &v[1..3];
    (v, s)
}
```
Even though, from a memory-layout point of view, this can be entirely safe
if the new location of the vector still lives longer than the lifetime `'a`
of the reference because the backing allocation of the vector does not change.

This library enables this safe usage by keeping the owner and the reference bundled together in a wrapper type that ensure that lifetime constraint:

```
fn return_owned_and_referenced() -> OwningRef<Vec<u8>, [u8]> {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
    let or = OwningRef::new(v);
    let or = or.map(|v| &v[1..3]);
    or
}
```
It works by requiring owner types to dereference to stable memory locations
and preventing mutable access to root containers, which in practice requires heap allocation
as provided by `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, etc.

Also provided are typedefs for common owner type combinations,
which allow for less verbose type signatures. For example, `BoxRef<T>` instead of `OwningRef<Box<T>, T>`.

The crate also provides the more advanced `OwningHandle` type,
which allows more freedom in bundling a dependent handle object
along with the data it depends on, at the cost of some unsafe needed in the API.
See the documentation around `OwningHandle` for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::BoxRef;
fn main() {
    // Create an array owned by a Box.
    let arr = Box::new([1, 2, 3, 4]) as Box<[i32]>;
    // Transfer into a BoxRef.
    let arr: BoxRef<[i32]> = BoxRef::new(arr);
    assert_eq!(&*arr, &[1, 2, 3, 4]);
    // We can slice the array without losing ownership or changing type.
    let arr: BoxRef<[i32]> = arr.map(|arr| &arr[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(&*arr, &[2, 3]);
    // Also works for Arc, Rc, String and Vec!
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#caching-a-reference-to-a-struct-field)Caching a reference to a struct field

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::BoxRef;
fn main() {
    struct Foo {
        tag: u32,
        x: u16,
        y: u16,
        z: u16,
    }
    let foo = Foo { tag: 1, x: 100, y: 200, z: 300 };
    let or = BoxRef::new(Box::new(foo)).map(|foo| {
        match foo.tag {
            0 => &foo.x,
            1 => &foo.y,
            2 => &foo.z,
            _ => panic!(),
        }
    });
    assert_eq!(*or, 200);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#caching-a-reference-to-an-entry-in-a-vector)Caching a reference to an entry in a vector

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::VecRef;
fn main() {
    let v = VecRef::new(vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).map(|v| &v[3]);
    assert_eq!(*v, 4);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#caching-a-subslice-of-a-string)Caching a subslice of a String

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::StringRef;
fn main() {
    let s = StringRef::new("hello world".to_owned())
        .map(|s| s.split(' ').nth(1).unwrap());
    assert_eq!(&*s, "world");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reference-counted-slices-that-share-ownership-of-the-backing-storage)Reference counted slices that share ownership of the backing storage

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::RcRef;
use std::rc::Rc;
fn main() {
    let rc: RcRef<[i32]> = RcRef::new(Rc::new([1, 2, 3, 4]) as Rc<[i32]>);
    assert_eq!(&*rc, &[1, 2, 3, 4]);
    let rc_a: RcRef<[i32]> = rc.clone().map(|s| &s[0..2]);
    let rc_b = rc.clone().map(|s| &s[1..3]);
    let rc_c = rc.clone().map(|s| &s[2..4]);
    assert_eq!(&*rc_a, &[1, 2]);
    assert_eq!(&*rc_b, &[2, 3]);
    assert_eq!(&*rc_c, &[3, 4]);
    let rc_c_a = rc_c.clone().map(|s| &s[1]);
    assert_eq!(&*rc_c_a, &4);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#atomic-reference-counted-slices-that-share-ownership-of-the-backing-storage)Atomic reference counted slices that share ownership of the backing storage

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::ArcRef;
use std::sync::Arc;
fn main() {
    use std::thread;
    fn par_sum(rc: ArcRef<[i32]>) -> i32 {
        if rc.len() == 0 {
            return 0;
        } else if rc.len() == 1 {
            return rc[0];
        }
        let mid = rc.len() / 2;
        let left = rc.clone().map(|s| &s[..mid]);
        let right = rc.map(|s| &s[mid..]);
        let left = thread::spawn(move || par_sum(left));
        let right = thread::spawn(move || par_sum(right));
        left.join().unwrap() + right.join().unwrap()
    }
    let rc: Arc<[i32]> = Arc::new([1, 2, 3, 4]);
    let rc: ArcRef<[i32]> = rc.into();
    assert_eq!(par_sum(rc), 10);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#references-into-raii-locks)References into RAII locks

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::RefRef;
use std::cell::{RefCell, Ref};
fn main() {
    let refcell = RefCell::new((1, 2, 3, 4));
    // Also works with Mutex and RwLock
    let refref = {
        let refref = RefRef::new(refcell.borrow()).map(|x| &x.3);
        assert_eq!(*refref, 4);
        // We move the RAII lock and the reference to one of
        // the subfields in the data it guards here:
        refref
    };
    assert_eq!(*refref, 4);
    drop(refref);
    assert_eq!(*refcell.borrow(), (1, 2, 3, 4));
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mutable-reference)Mutable reference

When the owned container implements `DerefMut`, it is also possible to make
a *mutable owning reference*. (E.g. with `Box`, `RefMut`, `MutexGuard`)

```
extern crate owning_ref;
use owning_ref::RefMutRefMut;
use std::cell::{RefCell, RefMut};
fn main() {
    let refcell = RefCell::new((1, 2, 3, 4));
    let mut refmut_refmut = {
        let mut refmut_refmut = RefMutRefMut::new(refcell.borrow_mut()).map_mut(|x| &mut x.3);
        assert_eq!(*refmut_refmut, 4);
        *refmut_refmut *= 2;
        refmut_refmut
    };
    assert_eq!(*refmut_refmut, 8);
    *refmut_refmut *= 2;
    drop(refmut_refmut);
    assert_eq!(*refcell.borrow(), (1, 2, 3, 16));
}
```

This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Erased](https://docs.rs/trait.Erased.html)
- Helper trait for an erased concrete type an owner dereferences to. This is used in form of a trait object for keeping something around to (virtually) call the destructor.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoErased.html)- Erased

for example `Box<T> -> Box<dyn Erased>`. This would be unneeded with higher kinded types support in the language.

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# memmap2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memmap2/latest/target-redirect/memmap2/

## Expand description

A cross-platform Rust API for memory mapped buffers.

The core functionality is provided by either [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) or

[, which correspond to mapping a](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)

`File`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&[u8]`[respectively. Both function by dereferencing to a slice, allowing the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&mut [u8]`[/](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)

`Mmap`[to be used in the same way you would the equivalent slice types.](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

For simple cases [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) can be used directly:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use memmap2::Mmap;
let mut file = File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?;
let mut contents = Vec::new();
file.read_to_end(&mut contents)?;
let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)?  };
assert_eq!(&contents[..], &mmap[..]);
```
However for cases which require configuration of the mapping, then
you can use [ MmapOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html) in order to further configure a mapping
before you create it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)
- A handle to an immutable memory mapped buffer.
- [MmapMut](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)
- A handle to a mutable memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html)- Options
- A memory map builder, providing advanced options and flags for specifying memory map behavior.
- [MmapRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRaw.html)
- A handle to a raw memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRawDescriptor.html)- RawDescriptor
- [Remap](https://docs.rs/struct.RemapOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `Mmap::remap``MmapMut::remap`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Advice](https://docs.rs/enum.Advice.html)
- Values supported by `Mmap::advise``MmapMut::advise`
- [Unchecked](https://docs.rs/enum.UncheckedAdvice.html)- Advice
- Values supported by `Mmap::unchecked_advise``MmapMut::unchecked_advise`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# smoldot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smoldot/2.1.0/smoldot/

## Expand description

Client for Polkadot and Substrate-compatible chains.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview-of-a-blockchain)Overview of a blockchain

A blockchain is, in its essence, a distributed and decentralized key-value database. The principle of a blockchain is to make it possible for any participant to perform modifications to this database, and for all participants to eventually agree on the current state of said database.

In Polkadot and Substrate-compatible chains, the state of this database is referred to as
“the storage”. The storage can be seen more or less as a very large `HashMap`.

A blockchain therefore consists in three main things:

- The initial state of the storage at the moment when the blockchain starts.
- A list of blocks, where each block represents a group of modifications performed to the storage.
- A peer-to-peer network of clients connected to each other and exchanging information such as newly-produced blocks.

Blocks are built on top of each other, forming a sequential list of modifications to the storage on top of its initial state.

[§](https://docs.rs#blocks)Blocks

A block primarily consists in three properties:

- A parent block, referred to by its hash.
- An ordered list of **extrinsics**, representing a state change about the storage. An extrinsic can be either a**transaction**or an**intrinsic**.
- A list of **digest log items**, which include information necessary to verify the authenticity of the block, such as a cryptographic signature of the block made by its author.

In order to make abstractions easier, there also exists what is called the **genesis block**,
or block number 0. It doesn’t have any parent, extrinsic, or digest item.

From these three block properties, the following other properties can be derived:

- The **hash**of the block. This is a unique 32 bytes identifier obtained by hashing all the block’s information together in a specific way.
- The **block number**. It is equal to the parent’s block number plus one, or equal to zero for the genesis block
- The state of the storage. It consists in the state of the storage of the parent block, on top of which the block’s extrinsics have been applied. The state of the storage of the genesis block is the initial state.

Note: Not all these properties are held in memory or even on disk. For instance, the state of the storage is quite large and holding a full version of the storage of every single block in the chain would be unrealistic.

[§](https://docs.rs#trie)Trie

The **trie** is a data structure that plays an important role in the way a blockchain
functions.

It consists in a tree of nodes associated with a key, some of these nodes containing a value.
Each node is associated with a hash called the **Merkle value** that encompasses the Merkle
values of the node’s children. The Merkle value of the root node of the tree is designated
as “the Merkle trie root” or “the trie root”.

See the [ trie](https://docs.rs/trie/index.html) module for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#block-headers)Block headers

In practical terms, when a block needs to be stored or transferred between machines, it
is split in two parts: a **header** and a **body**. The body of a block simply consists in its
list of extrinsics.

Note: The body of a block and the list of extrinsics of a block are the exact same thing, and these two designations can be used interchangeably.

A block’s header contains the following:

- The hash of the parent of the block.
- The block number.
- The **state trie root**, which consists in the trie root of all the keys and values of the storage of this block.
- The **extrinsics trie root**, which consists in the Merkle root of a trie containing the extrinsics of the block.
- The list of digest log items.

The hash of a block consists in the `blake2` hash of its header.

See the [ header](https://docs.rs/header/index.html) module for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime)Runtime

The state of the storage of each block is mostly opaque from the client’s perspective. There
exists, however, a few hard coded keys, the most important one being
`[0x3a, 0x63, 0x6f, 0x64, 0x65]` (which is the ASCII encoding of the string `:code`). The
value associated with this key must always be a [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/) binary
code called the **runtime**.

This WebAssembly binary code must obey a certain ABI and is responsible for the following actions:

- Verifying whether a block has been correctly created by its author.
- Providing the list of modifications to the storage performed by a block, given its header and body.
- Generating the header of newly-created blocks.
- Validating transactions received from third-parties, in order to later be potentially included in a block.
- Providing the tools necessary to create transactions.

In other words, the runtime is responsible for all the actual *logic* behind the chain being
run. For instance, when performing a transfer of tokens between one account and another, it is
the runtime WebAssembly code that verifies that the balances are correct and updates them.

Since applying an extrinsic modifies the state of the storage, it is possible for an
extrinsic to modify this WebAssembly binary code. This is called a **runtime upgrade**. In
other words, any block can potentially modify the logic of the chain.

See also the [ executor](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html) module for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#forks-and-finalization)Forks and finalization

While blocks are built on top of each other, they don’t necessarily form one single chain. It
is possible for multiple different blocks to have the same parent, thereby forming multiple
chains. This is called a **fork**.

When multiple chains fly around in the network, each node select one chain they consider as
the “best”. However, because of latency, disconnects, or similar reasons, it is possible for
a node to not be immediately aware of the existence of a chain that it would consider as a
better chain than its current best. Later, when this node learns about this better chain, it
will need to perform a **reorg** (short for *reorganization*), where blocks that were part of
the best chain no longer are.

In order to avoid troublesome situations arising from reorgs, Substrate/Polkadot provides the
concept of **finality**. Once a block has been finalized, it is guaranteed to always be part
of the best chain. By extension, the parent of a finalized block is always finalized as well.
The genesis block of a chain is by definition is always finalized.

As such, a chain of blocks is composed of two parts: one **finalized** part (usually the
longest), and one non-finalized part. While the finalized part is a single linear list of
blocks, the non-finalized part consists in a *directed rooted tree*.

In order to finalize a block, Substrate/Polkadot nodes use the **GrandPa** algorithm. Nodes
that are authorized to do so by the runtime emit votes on the peer-to-peer network. When two
thirds or more of the authorized nodes have voted for a specific block to be finalized, it
effectively becomes finalized.

After these votes have been collected, they are collected in what is called a
**justification**. This justification can later be requested by nodes who might not have
received all the votes, or for example if they were offline.

See the [ chain](https://docs.rs/chain/index.html) and

[modules for more information.](https://docs.rs/finality/index.html)

`finality`[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This library intentionally doesn’t provide any ready-to-use blockchain client. Instead, it provides tools that can be combined together in order to create a client.

Components that are most certainly needed are:

- Connectivity to a peer-to-peer network. See the `network`
- A persistent storage for the blocks. See the `database`
- A state machine that holds information about the state of the chain and verifies the
authenticity and/or correctness of blocks received from the network. See the `sync`

Optionally:

- The capacity to author new blocks. This isn’t implemented as of the writing of this documentation.
- A JSON-RPC client, in order to put a convenient-to-use UI on top of the client. See the
`json_rpc`
- TODO: telemetry

# kacrab_protocol - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kacrab-protocol/0.1.0/kacrab_protocol/

## Expand description

Kafka wire protocol — types, framing, record batches, compression, version negotiation.

[§](https://docs.rs#layout-1)Layout

Each module owns its data, its operations, and its error (`mod foo` →
`foo.rs` + `foo/error.rs`). The crate root re-exports the user-facing surface
and the symbols `generated/` references via `use crate::*`.

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `primitives` | Fixed-width int/float/bool + (un)signed varint(long) helpers. |
| `string` | + length-prefixed string read/write helpers.`KafkaString` |
| `bytes_io` | Length-prefixed raw byte read/write helpers. |
| `uuid` | + base64 URL-safe parsing (Java-compat).`KafkaUuid` |
| `tagged` | + flexible-version tagged-field section.`RawTaggedField` |
| `crc` | CRC32C compute + validation. |
| `frame` | TCP length-prefix framing + request encoding helpers. |
| `record` | Record batch v2: ,`RecordBatch`,`Record`.`RecordHeader` |
| `compression` | Codec dispatch (gzip/snappy/lz4/zstd, feature-gated). |
| `version` | API version resolution + header version selection. |
| `generated` | Codegen output (committed). One module per Kafka message. |

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

`#[from]`-converts
every module error so callers crossing layer boundaries can propagate

# urng - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/urng/0.5.3/urng/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#universal-rng)Universal RNG

A collection of random number generators.

This crate provides implementations of various pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs), including:

- **Mersenne Twister**:- `rng32::Mt19937`- `rng64::Mt1993764`
- **SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister**:- `rng32::Sfmt19937`- `rng64::Sfmt1993764`
- **Permuted Congruential Generator**:- `rng32::Pcg32`
- **Philox**:- `rng32::Philox32x4`- `rng64::Philox64`
- **Twisted Generalized Feedback Shift Register**:- `rng64::TwistedGFSR`
- **Small Fast Chaotic**:- `rng64::Sfc64`
- **Threefry**:- `rng32::Threefry32x4`- `rng32::Threefry32x2`
- **Threefish**:- `rng64::Threefish256`
- **Xorshift**:- `rng32::Xorshift32`- `rng64::Xorshift64`- `rng128::Xorshift128`] (128-bit state).
- **Xorwow**:- `rng32::Xorwow`
- **Xoshiro**(32-bit):- `rng32::Xoshiro128Pp`- `rng32::Xoshiro128Ss`
- **Xoshiro**(64-bit):- `rng64::Xoshiro256Pp`- `rng64::Xoshiro256Ss`
- **Xoroshiro**:- `rng64::xoroshiro::Xoroshiro128Pp`- `rng64::xoroshiro::Xoroshiro128Ss`
- **Linear Congruential Generator**:- `rng32::Lcg32`- `rng64::Lcg64`
- **Cet**:- `rng64::Cet64`- `rng64::Cet256`
- **SplitMix**:- `rng32::SplitMix32`- `rng64::SplitMix64`
- **Jenkins Small Fast**:- `rng32::Jsf32`

Each generator supports generating uniform random numbers for various types (u32, u64, f32, f64) and ranges.

# pallet_scored_pool - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pallet-scored-pool/48.0.0/pallet_scored_pool/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scored-pool-pallet)Scored Pool Pallet

The pallet maintains a scored membership pool. Each entity in the
pool can be attributed a `Score`. From this pool a set `Members`
is constructed. This set contains the `MemberCount` highest
scoring entities. Unscored entities are never part of `Members`.

If an entity wants to be part of the pool a deposit is required. The deposit is returned when the entity withdraws or when it is removed by an entity with the appropriate authority.

Every `Period` blocks the set of `Members` is refreshed from the
highest scoring members in the pool and, no matter if changes
occurred, `T::MembershipChanged::set_members_sorted` is invoked.
On first load `T::MembershipInitialized::initialize_members` is
invoked with the initial `Members` set.

It is possible to withdraw candidacy/resign your membership at any
time. If an entity is currently a member, this results in removal
from the `Pool` and `Members`; the entity is immediately replaced
by the next highest scoring candidate in the pool, if available.

[§](https://docs.rs#interface)Interface

[§](https://docs.rs#public-functions)Public Functions

- `submit_candidacy`- Submit candidacy to become a member. Requires a deposit.
- `withdraw_candidacy`- Withdraw candidacy. Deposit is returned.
- `score`- Attribute a quantitative score to an entity.
- `kick`- Remove an entity from the pool and members. Deposit is returned.
- `change_member_count`- Changes the amount of candidates taken into- `Members`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use pallet_scored_pool::{self as scored_pool};
#[frame_support::pallet]
pub mod pallet {
	use super::*;
	use frame_support::pallet_prelude::*;
	use frame_system::pallet_prelude::*;
	#[pallet::pallet]
	pub struct Pallet<T>(_);
	#[pallet::config]
	pub trait Config: frame_system::Config + scored_pool::Config {}
	#[pallet::call]
	impl<T: Config> Pallet<T> {
		#[pallet::weight({0})]
		pub fn candidate(origin: OriginFor<T>) -> DispatchResult {
			let who = ensure_signed(origin)?;
			let _ = <scored_pool::Pallet<T>>::submit_candidacy(
				T::RuntimeOrigin::from(Some(who.clone()).into())
			);
			Ok(())
		}
	}
}
```

This pallet depends on the [System pallet](https://docs.rs/frame_system/index.html).

# reifydb_profiler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reifydb-profiler/0.7.0/reifydb_profiler/

## Expand description

Always-on profiler primitives. Builds on `tracing` to capture per-scope span records without allocating on the hot
path. `ProfilerLayer` is a `tracing_subscriber::Layer` that intercepts spans matching a curated set of
`ProfilerCategory` prefixes, extracts numeric fields through reusable thread-local visitors, and appends a
fixed-size `MinimalSpanRecord` to scope-local state. `ProfilerScope::start` opens a scope; `ScopeHandle::finish`
drains the accumulated records, builds a `ProfilerSummary` for the caller, and hands the batch to a `ProfilerSink`
for downstream delivery (in production this is `sub-profiler`’s EventBus bridge).

This crate stays free of any metric or IoC dependency so the layer can be embedded in tests with a `NoopSink` and
so the rest of the workspace can use the data model without pulling in the subsystem.

# reifydb_column - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reifydb-column/0.7.0/reifydb_column/

## Expand description

Columnar storage engine: the immutable, on-disk representation of materialized columns plus the read-time machinery (compute kernels, predicates, scans, selection vectors, snapshots) the engine uses to query them. This crate owns the bucket layout and the per-column compression and encoding schemes.

Read paths come in here, get a column reader, and stream values through compute kernels that operate directly on the encoded bytes where possible - decoding only when a kernel cannot run on the encoded form. The snapshot type is what the subscription tier hands out to consumers so they can iterate over a stable view of the column without racing against ongoing writes.

Invariant: a column’s encoded bytes plus its stats and bitmap are produced together and never updated piecewise. Tearing those apart - rewriting just the values, just the bitmap, or just the stats - means readers can observe a column whose statistics no longer describe its contents, which silently corrupts every kernel that reads stats to skip work.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bucket](https://docs.rs/bucket/index.html)
- [compress](https://docs.rs/compress/index.html)
- [compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html)
- Compute kernels that operate on encoded columns. Compare, take, slice, filter, sum, search-sorted, min/max - the primitives the engine VM dispatches to when it executes the per-instruction work of a query. Kernels prefer to run directly on the encoded bytes (canonical layout, dictionary indices, run-length runs) and only decode when they cannot.
- [encoding](https://docs.rs/encoding/index.html)
- Per-column encoding implementations. Canonical is the dense unencoded layout; the compressed family covers all-none, bit-packed, constant, delta, delta-RLE, dictionary, frame-of-reference, run-length, and sparse forms. Each encoding produces and consumes the same encoded-bytes contract so compute kernels can be written once and work across encodings.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- [predicate](https://docs.rs/predicate/index.html)
- [reader](https://docs.rs/reader/index.html)
- [scan](https://docs.rs/scan/index.html)
- [selection](https://docs.rs/selection/index.html)
- [snapshot](https://docs.rs/snapshot/index.html)

# transmux - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/transmux/0.6.0/transmux/

## Expand description

`transmux` — MPEG-2 TS → CMAF/fMP4 container remux (ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015).

A **samples-in** container multiplexer: the caller supplies demuxed *coded*
access units + codec config, and `transmux` produces CMAF initialization and
media segments plus HLS playlists. It parses codec config/parameter headers
(SPS/PPS/VPS, AAC ASC, AC-3/E-AC-3 syncframe BSI) only to build the container
boxes and derive metadata — it never encodes or decodes media; coded samples
pass through opaque. `no_std` + `alloc`.

See the crate README for the full **feature matrix** (implemented boxes and
codecs plus planned coverage). Key entry points: [ build_init_segment](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.build_init_segment.html) and

[(batch),](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.build_media_segment.html)

`build_media_segment`[(streaming),](https://docs.rs/segmenter/struct.Segmenter.html)

`Segmenter`[with](https://docs.rs/nalu_types/struct.AvcSps.html#method.decode)

`AvcSps::decode`[(codec metadata), and the HLS playlist builders.](https://docs.rs/nalu_types/struct.AvcSps.html#method.rfc6381)

`AvcSps::rfc6381`This crate root also exposes the low-level ISOBMFF framing it is built on:
[ BoxHeader](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.BoxHeader.html) (optional 64-bit

`largesize` / `uuid` extended type),
[(](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.FullBoxHeader.html)

`FullBoxHeader``version` + `flags`), and a size-driven box walker
([) that skips unknown box types by advancing by](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.BoxIter.html)

`BoxIter``size`.[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use transmux::{box_iter, parse_box, BoxHeader, BoxType};
use broadcast_common::Parse;
// Parse a simple ftyp box header.
let bytes = [0, 0, 0, 12, b'f', b't', b'y', b'p', 0, 0, 0, 0];
let header = BoxHeader::parse(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(header.box_type.to_string(), "ftyp");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spec-citations)Spec citations

- **Box / FullBox**: ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §4.2 (fulltext L1254–L1304).
- **Box order**: §6.2.3 (recommendations; only- `ftyp`before variable-length and- `moof`sequence_number are mandatory).
- **Skip-unknown rule**: §4.2 L1294 — unknown type → ignore + skip via size.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

| Feature | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `std` | yes | `std::error::Error`impls |
| `serde` | yes | `serde::Serialize`for box types |

# memmap2 0.9.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memmap2/0.9.11

# memmap2

A Rust library for cross-platform memory mapped IO.

This is a **fork** of the [memmap-rs](https://github.com/danburkert/memmap-rs) crate.

## Features

- file-backed memory maps
- anonymous memory maps
- synchronous and asynchronous flushing
- copy-on-write memory maps
- read-only memory maps
-  stack support (`MAP_STACK`on unix)
- executable memory maps
- huge page support (linux only)

A list of supported/tested targets can be found in [Actions](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/memmap2-rs/actions).

## License

`memmap2` is primarily distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE), [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

Copyright (c) 2020 Yevhenii Reizner

Copyright (c) 2015 Dan Burkert

# memmap2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memmap2/0.9.11/target-redirect/memmap2/

## Expand description

A cross-platform Rust API for memory mapped buffers.

The core functionality is provided by either [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) or

[, which correspond to mapping a](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)

`File`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&[u8]`[respectively. Both function by dereferencing to a slice, allowing the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&mut [u8]`[/](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)

`Mmap`[to be used in the same way you would the equivalent slice types.](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

For simple cases [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) can be used directly:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use memmap2::Mmap;
let mut file = File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?;
let mut contents = Vec::new();
file.read_to_end(&mut contents)?;
let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)?  };
assert_eq!(&contents[..], &mmap[..]);
```
However for cases which require configuration of the mapping, then
you can use [ MmapOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html) in order to further configure a mapping
before you create it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)
- A handle to an immutable memory mapped buffer.
- [MmapMut](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)
- A handle to a mutable memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html)- Options
- A memory map builder, providing advanced options and flags for specifying memory map behavior.
- [MmapRaw](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRaw.html)
- A handle to a raw memory mapped buffer.
- [Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapRawDescriptor.html)- RawDescriptor
- [Remap](https://docs.rs/struct.RemapOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `Mmap::remap``MmapMut::remap`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Advice](https://docs.rs/enum.Advice.html)
- Values supported by `Mmap::advise``MmapMut::advise`
- [Unchecked](https://docs.rs/enum.UncheckedAdvice.html)- Advice
- Values supported by `Mmap::unchecked_advise``MmapMut::unchecked_advise`

[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// A memory map builder, providing advanced options and flags for specifying memory map behavior.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// `MmapOptions` can be used to create an anonymous memory map using [`map_anon()`], or a
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// file-backed memory map using one of [`map()`], [`map_mut()`], [`map_exec()`],
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// [`map_copy()`], or [`map_copy_read_only()`].
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// ## Safety
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// All file-backed memory map constructors are marked `unsafe` because of the potential for
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// *Undefined Behavior* (UB) using the map if the underlying file is subsequently modified, in or
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// out of process. Applications must consider the risk and take appropriate precautions when
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// using file-backed maps. Solutions such as file permissions, locks or process-private (e.g.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// unlinked) files exist but are platform specific and limited.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// [`map_anon()`]: MmapOptions::map_anon()
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// [`map()`]: MmapOptions::map()
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// [`map_mut()`]: MmapOptions::map_mut()
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// [`map_exec()`]: MmapOptions::map_exec()
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// [`map_copy()`]: MmapOptions::map_copy()
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// [`map_copy_read_only()`]: MmapOptions::map_copy_read_only()
[155](https://docs.rs#155)#[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)]
[156](https://docs.rs#156)pub struct MmapOptions {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    offset: u64,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    len: Option<usize>,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    huge: Option<u8>,
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    stack: bool,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    populate: bool,
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    no_reserve_swap: bool,
[163](https://docs.rs#163)}
[164](https://docs.rs#164)

[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// Creates a new set of options for configuring and creating a memory map.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// # Example
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    ///
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// ```
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// use memmap2::{MmapMut, MmapOptions};
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// # use std::io::Result;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    ///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// # fn main() -> Result<()> {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// // Create a new memory map builder.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// let mut mmap_options = MmapOptions::new();
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    ///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// // Configure the memory map builder using option setters, then create
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// // a memory map using one of `mmap_options.map_anon`, `mmap_options.map`,
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// // `mmap_options.map_mut`, `mmap_options.map_exec`, or `mmap_options.map_copy`:
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// let mut mmap: MmapMut = mmap_options.len(36).map_anon()?;
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    ///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// // Use the memory map:
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// mmap.copy_from_slice(b"...data to copy to the memory map...");
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// # Ok(())
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// # }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// ```
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    pub fn new() -> MmapOptions {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        MmapOptions::default()
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    }

[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// Configures the memory map to start at byte `offset` from the beginning of the file.

[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// By default, the offset is 0.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// # Example

[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// let mmap = unsafe {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    ///     MmapOptions::new()
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    ///                 .offset(30)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    ///                 .map(&File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?)?
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// };
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// assert_eq!(&b"Apache License"[..],

[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// ```

[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// Configures the created memory mapped buffer to be `len` bytes long.

[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// # Example
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    ///

[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// let mmap = unsafe {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    ///     MmapOptions::new()
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    ///                 .len(9)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    ///                 .map(&File::open("README.md")?)?
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// };
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// assert_eq!(&b"# memmap2"[..], &mmap[..]);

[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// # }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// ```
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    pub fn len(&mut self, len: usize) -> &mut Self {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        self.len = Some(len);
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        self
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    fn validate_len(len: u64) -> Result<usize> {
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        // Rust's slice cannot be larger than isize::MAX.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        // See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/slice/fn.from_raw_parts.html
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        //
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        // This is not a problem on 64-bit targets, but on 32-bit one
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        // having a file or an anonymous mapping larger than 2GB is quite normal
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        // and we have to prevent it.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        if isize::try_from(len).is_err() {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            return Err(Error::new(
[256](https://docs.rs#256)                ErrorKind::InvalidData,
[257](https://docs.rs#257)                "memory map length overflows isize",
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            ));
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        // If an unsigned number (u64) fits in isize, then it fits in usize.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        Ok(len as usize)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// Returns the configured length, or the length of the provided file.
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    fn get_len<T: MmapAsRawDesc>(&self, file: &T) -> Result<usize> {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        let len = if let Some(len) = self.len {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            len as u64
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        } else {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)            let desc = file.as_raw_desc();
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            let file_len = file_len(desc.0)?;
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)            if file_len < self.offset {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)                return Err(Error::new(
[274](https://docs.rs#274)                    ErrorKind::InvalidData,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)                    "memory map offset is larger than length",
[276](https://docs.rs#276)                ));
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            }
[278](https://docs.rs#278)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            file_len - self.offset
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        };
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        Self::validate_len(len)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }

[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// Configures the anonymous memory map to be allocated using huge pages.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// This option corresponds to the `MAP_HUGETLB` flag on Linux. It has no effect on Windows.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// The size of the requested page can be specified in page bits. If not provided, the system
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// default is requested. The requested length should be a multiple of this, or the mapping
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// will fail.
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    ///
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// This option has no effect on file-backed memory maps.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ///
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// # Example
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// ```
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// use memmap2::MmapOptions;
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    ///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// let stack = MmapOptions::new().huge(Some(21)).len(2*1024*1024).map_anon();
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// # Ok(())
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    /// # }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// ```
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    ///
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// The number 21 corresponds to `MAP_HUGE_2MB`. See mmap(2) for more details.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    pub fn huge(&mut self, page_bits: Option<u8>) -> &mut Self {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        self.huge = Some(page_bits.unwrap_or(0));
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        self
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    }

[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// Populate (prefault) page tables for a mapping.

[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// This option corresponds to the `MAP_POPULATE` flag on Linux. It has no effect on Windows.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    ///
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// # Example
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    ///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// ```
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// use memmap2::MmapOptions;
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// use std::fs::File;
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    ///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// let file = File::open("LICENSE-MIT")?;
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// let mmap = unsafe {

[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// };

[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// ```
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    pub fn populate(&mut self) -> &mut Self {
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        self.populate = true;
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        self
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// Do not reserve swap space for the memory map.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    ///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// By default, platforms may reserve swap space for memory maps.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// This guarantees that a write to the mapped memory will succeed, even if physical memory is exhausted.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Otherwise, the write to memory could fail (on Linux with a segfault).
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// This option requests that no swap space will be allocated for the memory map,
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// which can be useful for extremely large maps that are only written to sparsely.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// This option is currently supported on Linux, Android, Apple platforms (macOS, iOS, visionOS, etc.), NetBSD, Solaris and Illumos.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// On those platforms, this option corresponds to the `MAP_NORESERVE` flag.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// On Linux, this option is ignored if [`vm.overcommit_memory`](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/vm/overcommit-accounting) is set to 2.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    ///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// # Example
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    ///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// ```
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// use memmap2::MmapOptions;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// use std::fs::File;
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// let file = File::open("LICENSE-MIT")?;
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    ///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// let mmap = unsafe {
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    ///     MmapOptions::new().no_reserve_swap().map_copy(&file)?
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// };
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    /// assert_eq!(&b"Copyright"[..], &mmap[..9]);
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// # Ok(())
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// # }
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// ```
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    pub fn no_reserve_swap(&mut self) -> &mut Self {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        self.no_reserve_swap = true;
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        self
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    }
[394](https://docs.rs#394)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// Creates a read-only memory map backed by a file.
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// # Safety
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// See the [type-level][MmapOptions] docs for why this function is unsafe.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// # Errors
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// This method returns an error when the underlying system call fails, which can happen for a
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// variety of reasons, such as when the file is not open with read permissions.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// Returns [`ErrorKind::Unsupported`] on unsupported platforms.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    ///
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// # Example
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// ```
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// use memmap2::MmapOptions;
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// use std::fs::File;
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// use std::io::Read;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// let mut file = File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?;
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// let mut contents = Vec::new();
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// file.read_to_end(&mut contents)?;
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    ///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// let mmap = unsafe {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///     MmapOptions::new().map(&file)?
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// };
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    ///
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// assert_eq!(&contents[..], &mmap[..]);
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// # Ok(())
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// # }
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    pub unsafe fn map<T: MmapAsRawDesc>(&self, file: T) -> Result<Mmap> {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)        let desc = file.as_raw_desc();
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        MmapInner::map(
[433](https://docs.rs#433)            self.get_len(&file)?,
[434](https://docs.rs#434)            desc.0,

[678](https://docs.rs#678)
[679](https://docs.rs#679)/// A handle to an immutable memory mapped buffer.
[680](https://docs.rs#680)///
[681](https://docs.rs#681)/// A `Mmap` may be backed by a file, or it can be anonymous map, backed by volatile memory. Use
[682](https://docs.rs#682)/// [`MmapOptions`] or [`map()`] to create a file-backed memory map. To create an immutable
[683](https://docs.rs#683)/// anonymous memory map, first create a mutable anonymous memory map, and then make it immutable
[684](https://docs.rs#684)/// with [`MmapMut::make_read_only()`].
[685](https://docs.rs#685)///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)/// A file backed `Mmap` is created by `&File` reference, and will remain valid even after the
[687](https://docs.rs#687)/// `File` is dropped. In other words, the `Mmap` handle is completely independent of the `File`
[688](https://docs.rs#688)/// used to create it. For consistency, on some platforms this is achieved by duplicating the
[689](https://docs.rs#689)/// underlying file handle. The memory will be unmapped when the `Mmap` handle is dropped.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)///
[691](https://docs.rs#691)/// Dereferencing and accessing the bytes of the buffer may result in page faults (e.g. swapping
[692](https://docs.rs#692)/// the mapped pages into physical memory) though the details of this are platform specific.
[693](https://docs.rs#693)///
[694](https://docs.rs#694)/// `Mmap` is [`Sync`] and [`Send`].
[695](https://docs.rs#695)///
[696](https://docs.rs#696)/// See [`MmapMut`] for the mutable version.
[697](https://docs.rs#697)///
[698](https://docs.rs#698)/// ## Safety
[699](https://docs.rs#699)///
[700](https://docs.rs#700)/// All file-backed memory map constructors are marked `unsafe` because of the potential for
[701](https://docs.rs#701)/// *Undefined Behavior* (UB) using the map if the underlying file is subsequently modified, in or
[702](https://docs.rs#702)/// out of process. Applications must consider the risk and take appropriate precautions when using
[703](https://docs.rs#703)/// file-backed maps. Solutions such as file permissions, locks or process-private (e.g. unlinked)
[704](https://docs.rs#704)/// files exist but are platform specific and limited.
[705](https://docs.rs#705)///
[706](https://docs.rs#706)/// ## Example
[707](https://docs.rs#707)///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)/// ```
[709](https://docs.rs#709)/// use memmap2::MmapOptions;
[710](https://docs.rs#710)/// use std::io::Write;
[711](https://docs.rs#711)/// use std::fs::File;
[712](https://docs.rs#712)///
[713](https://docs.rs#713)/// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[714](https://docs.rs#714)/// let file = File::open("README.md")?;
[715](https://docs.rs#715)/// let mmap = unsafe { MmapOptions::new().map(&file)? };
[716](https://docs.rs#716)/// assert_eq!(b"# memmap2", &mmap[0..9]);
[717](https://docs.rs#717)/// # Ok(())
[718](https://docs.rs#718)/// # }
[719](https://docs.rs#719)/// ```
[720](https://docs.rs#720)///
[721](https://docs.rs#721)/// [`map()`]: Mmap::map()
[722](https://docs.rs#722)pub struct Mmap {
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    inner: MmapInner,
[724](https://docs.rs#724)}
[725](https://docs.rs#725)
[726](https://docs.rs#726)impl Mmap {
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    /// Creates a read-only memory map backed by a file.

[739](https://docs.rs#739)    ///
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// Returns [`ErrorKind::Unsupported`] on unsupported platforms.

[795](https://docs.rs#795)    /// let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? };
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    /// // ... use the read-only memory map ...
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    /// let mut mut_mmap = mmap.make_mut()?;

[801](https://docs.rs#801)    /// ```
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    pub fn make_mut(mut self) -> Result<MmapMut> {

[999](https://docs.rs#999)    /// Flushes outstanding memory map modifications to disk.
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    ///
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    /// When this method returns with a non-error result, all outstanding changes to a file-backed
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    /// memory map are guaranteed to be durably stored. The file's metadata (including last
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    /// modification timestamp) may not be updated.
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    ///
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    /// # Example
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    ///
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)    /// ```
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)    /// use std::fs::OpenOptions;
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)    /// use std::io::Write;
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)    /// use std::path::PathBuf;
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)    /// use std::slice;
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)    ///
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)    /// use memmap2::MmapRaw;
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)    ///
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)    /// # fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)    /// let tempdir = tempfile::tempdir()?;
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)    /// let path: PathBuf = /* path to file */
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)    /// #   tempdir.path().join("flush");
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)    /// let file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(&path)?;
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)    /// file.set_len(128)?;
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)    ///
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)    /// let mut mmap = unsafe { MmapRaw::map_raw(&file)? };
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)    ///
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)    /// let mut memory = unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts_mut(mmap.as_mut_ptr(), 128) };
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)    /// memory.write_all(b"Hello, world!")?;
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)    /// mmap.flush()?;
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)    /// # Ok(())
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)    /// # }
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)    /// ```
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    pub fn flush(&self) -> Result<()> {
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)        let len = self.len();
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)        self.inner.flush(0, len)
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)    }
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)

[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)/// A handle to a mutable memory mapped buffer.
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)///
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)/// A file-backed `MmapMut` buffer may be used to read from or write to a file. An anonymous
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)/// `MmapMut` buffer may be used any place that an in-memory byte buffer is needed. Use
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)/// [`MmapMut::map_mut()`] and [`MmapMut::map_anon()`] to create a mutable memory map of the
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)/// respective types, or [`MmapOptions::map_mut()`] and [`MmapOptions::map_anon()`] if non-default
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)/// options are required.
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)///
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)/// A file backed `MmapMut` is created by `&File` reference, and will remain valid even after the
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)/// `File` is dropped. In other words, the `MmapMut` handle is completely independent of the `File`
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)/// used to create it. For consistency, on some platforms this is achieved by duplicating the
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)/// underlying file handle. The memory will be unmapped when the `MmapMut` handle is dropped.
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)///
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)/// Dereferencing and accessing the bytes of the buffer may result in page faults (e.g. swapping
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)/// the mapped pages into physical memory) though the details of this are platform specific.
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)///
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)/// `MmapMut` is [`Sync`] and [`Send`].
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)///
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)/// See [`Mmap`] for the immutable version.
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)///
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)/// ## Safety
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)///
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)/// All file-backed memory map constructors are marked `unsafe` because of the potential for
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)/// *Undefined Behavior* (UB) using the map if the underlying file is subsequently modified, in or
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)/// out of process. Applications must consider the risk and take appropriate precautions when using
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)/// file-backed maps. Solutions such as file permissions, locks or process-private (e.g. unlinked)
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)/// files exist but are platform specific and limited.
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)pub struct MmapMut {
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    inner: MmapInner,
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)}
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)impl MmapMut {
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    /// Creates a writeable memory map backed by a file.
